plain: The city's main account for everyday services like police, fire, parks and libraries, paid for mostly by local taxes. It is the part of the budget the City Council has the most freedom to spend.

Money the city can count on only once, such as savings left over from last year or a temporary federal grant. Using it to pay for costs that come back every year leaves a hole in the next year's budget.
The amount by which the city's regular yearly costs are bigger than its regular yearly income. One-time money can cover it for a year, but it comes back until costs are cut or income goes up.

A deposit into the city's rainy-day savings, kept for emergencies and economic downturns. Skipping the deposit makes one year's budget easier to balance but leaves the savings further below the city's own target.

Short for actuarially determined contribution: the yearly payment into the city employees' pension fund that the pension system's actuary says is required to pay for promised retirement benefits. San Diego has paid the full amount every year since FY2006, so each budget includes it in full.
